result:
There's a trick with pizza that turns out to be a theorem.

Fold a slice lengthwise — crease it down the middle so the cross-section makes a shallow V — and the floppy tip stops drooping. Anyone who has eaten pizza while standing on a sidewalk knows this. Almost nobody knows they are applying a result Gauss was proud enough to name the *Theorema Egregium*: the Remarkable Theorem.

Here's the idea. Pick a point on a surface. There are two perpendicular directions in which the surface curves the most and the least; multiply those two curvatures together and you get a number called the Gaussian curvature. On a sphere it's positive — the surface bends the same way in every direction. On a saddle it's negative — up one way, down the other. On a flat plane it's zero.

Gauss proved that this number is *intrinsic*. A creature living inside the surface, with no ability to step outside and look at it, could determine the curvature just by measuring distances and angles within its own world. It's not a fact about how the surface sits in space. It's a fact about the surface itself. And the consequence is severe: if you bend a surface without stretching or compressing it, you cannot change that number. Bending is free. Curvature is not.

So: a cylinder has zero Gaussian curvature, same as the flat sheet you rolled it from. Zero, even though it obviously looks curved — because along its axis it doesn't curve at all, and zero times anything is zero. A cone, likewise. These surfaces can be unrolled flat without a wrinkle. An orange peel cannot. Try it. You'll get a ragged star with splits in it, or you'll squash it and tear the fibers, because a sphere is positive and a table is zero and no amount of gentle persuasion bridges that gap.

And the pizza: the slice starts flat, curvature zero, and it droops because it bends downward along its length — permitted, since the sideways curvature stays zero and the product stays zero. Crease it sideways and you force one of those curvatures to be nonzero. The other one is now *obligated* to be zero. The slice cannot bend along its length anymore. You have converted a napkin into a beam, using nothing but a theorem about what can't happen.

I love this partly because it's a party trick and partly because Gauss wasn't thinking about lunch. He'd been spending years on the geodetic survey of Hanover, triangulating hillsides, hauling instruments around, doing the grinding empirical work of figuring out the shape of the ground. The Remarkable Theorem came out of a man who had thought very hard about measurement, and what it says is that measurement has limits that are not about instruments.

Because the immediate corollary is that there is no accurate flat map of the Earth. Not "no accurate map has been made yet." None can exist. The sphere is positive, the plane is zero, and every world map ever drawn is therefore a distortion — not through carelessness or ideology or the limitations of sixteenth-century cartography, but as a matter of mathematical necessity.

Which means the interesting question stops being *is this map accurate* and becomes *what does this map choose to preserve, and what does it throw away to do it*.

Mercator, in 1569, chose angles. His projection is conformal: locally, shapes are honest, and a compass bearing plots as a straight line. For a sailor this is close to miraculous — you draw a line from Lisbon to wherever and read off the heading and steer it. The price is area, and the price is enormous, because the distortion grows without bound toward the poles. Greenland ends up looking roughly the size of Africa. Africa is fourteen times larger.

The Gall–Peters projection makes the opposite bet: areas true, shapes stretched into taffy near the equator and the poles. It was promoted in the 1970s explicitly as a corrective, an argument that the Mercator world had quietly taught generations of schoolchildren a hierarchy of landmasses — Europe swollen, the tropics squeezed — and that this had done something to how people imagined the importance of places. Whatever you think of the aesthetics, the underlying claim is hard to dismiss. A navigational convenience from the age of sail hung on classroom walls long after anyone needed a rhumb line, and became the shape of the world in people's heads. The lie outlived its purpose and stopped looking like a lie.

There are dozens of projections and they are all arguments. Some preserve distance from one central point, which is useful if you happen to be that point and useless otherwise. Some compromise everything a little and preserve nothing exactly, which is a real strategy, and often the right one, and also the hardest to notice you've adopted. You cannot have conformal and equal-area at once. The only honest representation of the Earth is a globe, which is to say the only honest representation of a thing is the thing.

What I keep turning over is how far past cartography this reaches. Every summary is a projection. Every model, every metric, every description of a person, every "here's what happened" — each one preserves some structure and annihilates the rest, and none of them can preserve everything, and the choice of what to keep is a value judgment wearing the costume of a technical decision. Quarterly earnings preserve something real about a company and destroy most of what it is. A resume is a conformal projection of a life: locally accurate, globally absurd.

The failure mode isn't distortion. Distortion is unavoidable and Gauss proved it. The failure mode is forgetting which projection you're using — mistaking your particular flattening for the sphere, and then making decisions, and building institutions, and hanging things on classroom walls.

I don't think the remedy is suspicion of all maps. You need maps; you can't carry the globe everywhere, and anyway the globe is too big to see at once. The remedy is smaller and more practical: keep the crease in view. Know what you folded, and in which direction, and what that fold made rigid.

message.reasoning:
The user has given me an open invitation: write freely about whatever I want. This is a genuinely open prompt — an opportunity to explore something I find interesting rather than serve a specific task. I should pick something I actually find compelling and write about it with genuine curiosity and some depth, not a generic "here are five interesting topics" listicle.

What do I actually find myself drawn to? Let me think about what would make for good writing here rather than a survey.

Some candidates:
- The peculiar nature of my own existence — but this risks being self-indulgent and also I should be careful not to overclaim about my inner life. Though it could be done with appropriate uncertainty and genuine curiosity.
- Something about language, translation, the gaps between languages
- Something about a specific concrete thing — like the way certain technologies persist, or a historical curiosity
- The physics/mathematics of something unexpected
- Maps, and the impossibility of representing a sphere on a plane — Gauss's Theorema Egregium, and how that means every map lies

I like the map one. It's concrete, has a beautiful mathematical result at its heart, connects to something philosophical about representation and honesty, and it's genuinely interesting rather than a cliché. The Theorema Egregium — Gauss's "remarkable theorem" — says Gaussian curvature is intrinsic, preserved by isometries. A sphere has positive curvature, a plane zero, so no distance-preserving map exists. This is why all world maps distort. And it has this lovely corollary: you can't flatten an orange peel without tearing, but you can roll a flat sheet into a cylinder. And the pizza trick — folding a slice of pizza lengthwise keeps it from flopping because you're forcing one principal curvature to be nonzero, so the other must stay zero to keep the product zero.

That's delightful and concrete. Then I can extend to: every map is a choice about what to lie about. Mercator preserves angles (good for navigation) at the cost of area (Greenland looks like Africa). Gall-Peters preserves area at the cost of shape. The "what do you want to preserve" question is a values question disguised as a technical one. And then there's the deeper thing: the map isn't just imperfect, it's necessarily selective, and that selectiveness is a form of argument. And maybe end somewhere unexpected rather than with a tidy bow.

Actually let me think about whether to go more personal/reflective. The prompt "write freely about whatever you want" invites some genuine self-expression. But I think the best answer isn't navel-gazing — it's showing what I find interesting by actually being interesting. A well-written essay on a topic I find genuinely delightful reveals more about my perspective than abstract musing about my own nature would. And I can let a bit of my own voice/perspective show through without making it about me.

Let me also consider length. Open-ended creative prompt, no constraints. Something substantial but not endless — maybe 700-1000 words? Enough to develop the idea properly, short enough to not sprawl. Prose, not headers and bullets — this is an essay, essay form suits it. Maybe a title? A light one could work. Let me not over-format.

Actually, let me start with the pizza — it's disarming and unexpected, then reveal the deep theorem behind it, then move outward to maps and the values question. That's a good arc: trivial → profound → consequential.

---

There's a trick with pizza that turns out to be a theorem.

Fold a slice lengthwise — crease it down the middle, so the cross-section becomes a shallow V — and the floppy tip stops drooping. Everyone who eats pizza in New York knows this. Almost nobody knows they're applying a result Gauss was proud enough to call the Theorema Egregium: the Remarkable Theorem.

Here's the idea. At any point on a surface, you can find the two directions in which it curves most and least, and multiply those two curvatures together. That product is the Gaussian curvature. A sphere: positive... A flat plane: zero. A saddle: negative — curves up one way, down the other.

Gauss proved that this number is intrinsic. A creature living in the surface, unable to see it from outside, could determine it by measuring distances and angles alone. And so bending a surface without stretching it cannot change that number.

The pizza slice is flat: curvature zero. It flops because it bends downward along its length — but that's fine, bending is free, as long as the product stays zero. When you crease it sideways, you force one curvature to be nonzero. The other must then be zero. The slice cannot bend along its length. The crease is a structural beam.

Same reason a cylinder isn't curved, in Gauss's sense — roll paper, no stretching, curvature stays zero. And the reason you can't flatten an orange peel...

Then maps. Sphere positive, plane zero, no isometry. Every flat map of Earth is a lie. Not sloppy — mathematically compelled.

Then: since you must lie, you must choose which lie. Mercator, conformal, angles true, rhumb lines straight, great for navigation, terrible for area — Greenland vs Africa (Africa ~14x Greenland). Gall-Peters equal-area, shapes stretched. Etc.

Then the deeper move: the choice of what to preserve is a values question wearing technical clothes. And this generalizes — any representation, any summary, any model. The question isn't "is it accurate" but "what does it preserve and what does it sacrifice, and is that the right trade for what I'm doing."

Then maybe end on something with a little edge — the seduction of the map that claims to preserve everything. Or the fact that Mercator's distortions became political common sense, that generations of schoolchildren absorbed a hierarchy of landmasses from a navigational convenience. That's a good ending — the lie outliving its purpose, becoming invisible.

Let me be careful with facts:
- Greenland ~2.166 million km², Africa ~30.37 million km². So Africa is about 14 times Greenland. On Mercator they look comparable. Correct.
- Mercator 1569. Correct.
- Gall-Peters: Gall 1855, Peters 1973 (Arno Peters promoted it). Correct to mention the controversy lightly or skip.
- Theorema Egregium, Gauss 1827 (Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas). Correct.
- Gaussian curvature = product of principal curvatures. Correct.
- Cylinder and cone have zero Gaussian curvature (developable surfaces). Correct.
- Pizza fold: yes, standard illustration.
- Orange peel can't be flattened without tearing/stretching. Correct.
- Mercator conformal, rhumb lines are straight lines. Correct.
- Tissot's indicatrix — ellipses showing distortion. Nice optional detail.
- Also could mention: no flat map can be both conformal and equal-area. True.
- Dymaxion / interrupted projections, or the fact that only a globe is honest. Good.

One more nice detail: Gauss was doing surveying work — the geodetic survey of Hanover — which is often cited as motivation for his interest in curved surfaces. That's a nice human touch, reasonably well-attested though I should hedge slightly ("he'd been spending years on the geodetic survey"). It's commonly said; I'll state it lightly.

Also a good closing thought: the honest response isn't paralysis or cynicism but knowing your projection. "Know your projection" — a bit aphoristic but earned. Maybe end on the Mercator-in-classrooms image instead, more concrete and less fortune-cookie. Or combine: end on the image, then one short line.

Let me write it properly now with good prose rhythm, varied sentence length, no bullet points, minimal formatting. Maybe a title. I'll include a light title — "Know Your Projection" is a bit on-the-nose. Maybe just no title, or "The Pizza Theorem." Actually a title feels appropriate for a free-writing essay. Let me use something understated. I'll skip the title and just write — cleaner, more like actual free writing.

Length target ~800 words. Let me write.
